q: Non-metals are the chemical elements that mostly lack the characteristics of metals.
e: This is the exact definition of non-metals provided in the textbook.

q: Non-metals are located on the left side of the Periodic Table.
e: Non-metals are located on the right side of the Periodic Table.

q: Among non-metals, 6 non-metals are solids, and 11 non-metals are gases.
e: The textbook states there are 6 solid non-metals and 11 gaseous non-metals.

q: Only one non-metal, chlorine, is a liquid.
e: Only one non-metal, bromine, is a liquid.

q: Nitrogen is the non-metallic element with the symbol N and atomic number 7.
e: Nitrogen has the symbol N and atomic number 7.

q: A nitrogen atom has 7 protons, 7 neutrons, and 7 electrons.
e: The textbook specifies that a nitrogen atom has 7 protons, 7 neutrons, and 7 electrons.

q: A nitrogen molecule has two nitrogen atoms joined together by two covalent bonds.
e: A nitrogen molecule has two nitrogen atoms joined together by three covalent bonds.

q: Nitrogen is a colourless gas with a pungent smell.
e: Nitrogen is a colourless gas without any smell and is very unreactive.

q: Nitrogen has a very low boiling point of -196°C.
e: The textbook states the boiling point of nitrogen is -196°C.

q: The Earth's atmosphere is made up of 78 percentage of nitrogen.
e: Nitrogen makes up 78% of the Earth's atmosphere.

q: There is a large amount of nitrogen in the Earth's crust.
e: Even though there is so much nitrogen in the air, there is very little in the Earth's crust.

q: Nitrogen can be found in fairly rare minerals such as Chile saltpetre ($NaNO_3$).
e: Chile saltpetre ($NaNO_3$) is mentioned as a rare mineral containing nitrogen.

q: Industrially, elemental nitrogen can be manufactured by fractional distillation of liquid air.
e: Fractional distillation of liquid air is the industrial method for manufacturing elemental nitrogen.

q: In the preparation of nitrogen from air, caustic soda solution is used to remove oxygen.
e: Caustic soda solution is used to remove carbon dioxide, not oxygen.

q: Carbon dioxide free air is passed over heated copper which absorbs oxygen to form copper(II) oxide.
e: Heated copper absorbs oxygen to form copper(II) oxide, freeing the nitrogen.

q: Nitrogen gas is collected by the upward displacement of water.
e: Since nitrogen is only slightly soluble in water, it is collected by the downward displacement of water.

q: If dry nitrogen is required, it may be passed through a U-tube containing glass beads wetted with concentrated sulphuric acid.
e: Concentrated sulphuric acid is used to dry the nitrogen gas.

q: The main use of nitrogen is in the manufacture of ammonia gas.
e: The textbook states the main use of nitrogen is in the manufacture of ammonia gas.

q: Some important nitrogen fertilisers are ammonium nitrate, ammonium sulphate, and urea.
e: These three compounds are explicitly listed as important nitrogen fertilisers.

q: Since nitrogen has 5 electrons in its outermost shell, its oxidation numbers vary from -3 to +5.
e: The 5 outermost electrons allow nitrogen to have oxidation numbers ranging from -3 to +5.

q: The oxidation number of nitrogen in ammonia ($NH_3$) is -3.
e: Table 6.1 lists the oxidation number of nitrogen in ammonia as -3.

q: The oxidation number of nitrogen in dinitrogen oxide ($N_2O$) is +2.
e: The oxidation number of nitrogen in dinitrogen oxide ($N_2O$) is +1.

q: The oxidation number of nitrogen in nitric acid ($HNO_3$) is +5.
e: Table 6.1 lists the oxidation number of nitrogen in nitric acid as +5.

q: Some common oxides of nitrogen are dinitrogen oxide, nitrogen oxide, and nitrogen dioxide.
e: These three are the common oxides of nitrogen discussed in the textbook.

q: Dinitrogen oxide is collected by the downward displacement of hot water.
e: Table 6.2 states dinitrogen oxide is collected by the downward displacement of hot water.

q: Dinitrogen oxide is a reddish-brown gas with a pungent odour.
e: Dinitrogen oxide is a colourless gas with a sweetish odour.

q: Nitrogen oxide is collected by the downward displacement of cold water.
e: Table 6.2 states nitrogen oxide is collected by the downward displacement of cold water.

q: Nitrogen oxide is soluble in water.
e: Nitrogen oxide is insoluble in water.

q: Nitrogen dioxide is collected by the upward displacement of air.
e: Table 6.2 states nitrogen dioxide is collected by the upward displacement of air.

q: Nitrogen dioxide is a colourless gas with a pungent and irritating smell.
e: Nitrogen dioxide is a reddish-brown gas with a pungent and irritating smell.

q: Dinitrogen oxide is readily decomposed above 600°C into nitrogen and oxygen.
e: The textbook states dinitrogen oxide decomposes above 600°C to nitrogen and oxygen.

q: At -10°C, nitrogen dioxide exists as a solid, colourless dimer molecule, dinitrogen tetroxide ($N_2O_4$).
e: Nitrogen dioxide forms the colourless dimer dinitrogen tetroxide at -10°C.

q: At about 150°C, $NO_2$ begins to dissociate into colourless nitrogen oxide and oxygen.
e: The textbook states that at about 150°C, $NO_2$ dissociates into nitrogen oxide and oxygen.

q: Dinitrogen oxide supports combustion as actively as oxygen and it produces nitrogen when heated.
e: Dinitrogen oxide actively supports combustion, producing nitrogen.

q: A cold acidified solution of iron(II) sulphate is poured into a gas jar of nitrogen oxide to give a brown nitroso iron(II) sulphate solution.
e: This reaction forms the brown nitroso complex, a test for nitrogen oxide.

q: Nitrogen oxide combines directly with chlorine in the presence of charcoal to form yellow nitrosyl chloride gas.
e: The textbook states this combination forms yellow nitrosyl chloride gas.

q: Nitrogen dioxide dissolves in water to form a mixture of nitric acid and nitrous acid.
e: The dissolution of nitrogen dioxide in water yields both nitric and nitrous acids.

q: When nitrogen dioxide reacts with aqueous alkalis, the corresponding nitrates and nitrites are formed.
e: Reaction with aqueous alkalis produces both nitrates and nitrites.

q: Dinitrogen oxide gas is also known as laughing gas and is used as an anaesthetic for minor surgical operations.
e: Dinitrogen oxide is commonly called laughing gas and used as an anaesthetic.

q: Ammonia is the most thermally stable hydride of nitrogen.
e: The textbook identifies ammonia as the most thermally stable hydride of nitrogen.

q: In the Haber process, nitrogen and hydrogen gases are mixed together in the ratio of 1:3 by volume.
e: The Haber process uses a 1:3 volume ratio of nitrogen to hydrogen.

q: The Haber process uses an iron catalyst at a high pressure of about 200 atm and a moderately high temperature of 450°C.
e: These are the exact conditions specified for the Haber process.

q: In the laboratory preparation of ammonia gas, an excess of slaked lime and ammonium chloride are mixed and heated.
e: This is the standard laboratory method for preparing ammonia gas.

q: Ammonia gas is dried by passage through a drying tower which contains the drying agent quicklime ($CaO$).
e: Quicklime ($CaO$) is the specified drying agent for ammonia gas.

q: Ammonia gas is collected by the upward displacement of air.
e: Since ammonia is lighter than air, it is collected by the downward displacement of air.

q: Ammonia gas should not be dried by usual drying agents such as anhydrous calcium chloride, concentrated sulphuric acid, and phosphorus(V) oxide.
e: These compounds react with ammonia and therefore cannot be used to dry it.

q: Ammonia is a colourless gas with a characteristic pungent smell.
e: This matches the physical description of ammonia gas in the textbook.

q: Liquid ammonia boils at 33.3°C and freezes at -77.7°C.
e: Liquid ammonia boils at -33.3°C and freezes at -77.7°C.

q: The solubility of ammonia gas in water is often demonstrated in the laboratory by the 'Fountain experiment'.
e: The Fountain experiment is the standard demonstration for ammonia's extreme solubility.

q: When ammonia gas reacts with hydrogen chloride gas, dense white fumes of solid ammonium chloride are observed.
e: This reaction produces dense white fumes of ammonium chloride.

q: When ammonia is passed over heated copper(II) oxide, it reduces the copper(II) oxide to copper.
e: Ammonia acts as a reducing agent, reducing copper(II) oxide to copper.

q: When excess ammonia reacts with chlorine, nitrogen trichloride is obtained.
e: When excess ammonia reacts with chlorine, nitrogen is obtained; nitrogen trichloride is formed if chlorine is in excess.

q: Dry ammonia passed over sodium metal heated to red heat forms sodium amide.
e: The reaction of dry ammonia with heated sodium metal produces sodium amide.

q: Magnesium reacts with dry ammonia to form magnesium amide.
e: Magnesium reacts with dry ammonia to form magnesium nitride, not magnesium amide.

q: Both sodium amide and magnesium nitride are hydrolysed by water to regenerate ammonia.
e: Hydrolysis of both compounds regenerates ammonia gas.

q: Ammonia is used in the manufacture of fertilisers, plastics, explosives, textiles, pesticides, dyes, and other chemicals.
e: This is the comprehensive list of ammonia uses provided in the textbook.

q: Nitric acid is known as aqua fortis, which is Latin for 'strong water'.
e: The textbook states nitric acid is known as aqua fortis, meaning 'strong water'.

q: Nitric acid is manufactured by the Ammonia Oxidation Process.
e: The Ammonia Oxidation Process is the industrial method for manufacturing nitric acid.

q: In the Ammonia Oxidation Process, ammonia and oxygen react over a Pt-Rh catalyst at red heat to form nitrogen oxide and water.
e: This is the first step of the Ammonia Oxidation Process.

q: The nitrogen oxide formed is rapidly cooled and made to combine with oxygen from excess air to form nitrogen dioxide.
e: Nitrogen oxide combines with oxygen to form reddish-brown nitrogen dioxide.

q: Nitric acid should be stored in brown glass bottles because it decomposes when subject to heat or light.
e: Decomposition by heat or light necessitates storage in brown glass bottles.

q: Dilute nitric acid neutralises bases, forming nitrates and water.
e: This is the standard acidic property of dilute nitric acid.

q: Nitric acid oxidises metals to give metal nitrates, water, and oxides of nitrogen.
e: This describes the oxidising property of nitric acid with metals.

q: With reactive metals such as magnesium and dilute nitric acid, nitrogen dioxide gas is liberated.
e: With reactive metals such as magnesium and dilute nitric acid, hydrogen gas is liberated.

q: With less reactive metals such as zinc or aluminium and hot dilute nitric acid, hydrogen gas is produced.
e: With less reactive metals such as zinc or aluminium and hot dilute nitric acid, ammonium nitrate is produced.

q: Aqua regia is a mixture of 3 volumes concentrated hydrochloric acid and 1 volume concentrated nitric acid.
e: This is the exact volume ratio for aqua regia given in the Key Terms.

q: The ability of aqua regia to dissolve gold is due to the oxidation of hydrochloric acid by nitric acid to liberate chlorine.
e: The liberated chlorine converts gold into gold(III) chloride, which then dissolves.

q: Sulphur is the non-metallic solid element with the symbol S and atomic number 16.
e: The textbook defines sulphur with the symbol S and atomic number 16.

q: A sulphur atom has 16 protons, 16 neutrons, and 16 electrons, with 6 electrons in its outermost shell.
e: This matches the electronic structure description of the sulphur atom.

q: Nowadays most sulphur is obtained from the sulphur compounds found in petroleum and natural gas.
e: The textbook states this is the primary modern source of sulphur.

q: Sulphur is widely found in nature as iron pyrites (iron sulphide), galena (lead(II) sulphide), gypsum (calcium sulphate), and epsom salts (magnesium sulphate).
e: These are the specific mineral forms of sulphur listed in the text.

q: The structural unit in the solid state of sulphur is the $S_8$ ring structure.
e: The $S_8$ ring is the fundamental structural unit of solid sulphur.

q: There are three allotropic forms of sulphur: rhombic, monoclinic, and plastic sulphur.
e: These are the three allotropes of sulphur described in the textbook.

q: When a solution of sulphur in carbon disulphide is allowed to evaporate slowly at room temperature, octahedral crystals of rhombic sulphur are deposited.
e: This is the described method for obtaining rhombic sulphur.

q: Molten sulphur poured into a wet filter paper in a funnel forms long, dark yellow, needle-like crystals of monoclinic sulphur.
e: This accurately describes the formation of monoclinic sulphur crystals.

q: Monoclinic sulphur slowly changes into the rhombic form at temperatures below 96°C (369K), which is the transition temperature.
e: 96°C (369K) is the transition temperature where monoclinic sulphur converts to rhombic sulphur.

q: Plastic sulphur is formed when any form of sulphur is heated almost to its boiling point and then poured into cold water.
e: This is the exact method described for forming plastic sulphur.

q: In plastic sulphur, the $S_8$ ring molecules are ruptured and the sulphur atoms join together to form long chains with a zig-zag arrangement.
e: This describes the structural difference of plastic sulphur from crystalline forms.

q: Sulphur deposited at about 700 ft (~213 m) below the Earth's surface is extracted by the Frasch Process.
e: The Frasch Process is used for extracting deep underground sulphur deposits.

q: In the Frasch Process, superheated steam at about 160°C is forced down under pressure through the outermost pipe to melt the sulphur.
e: Superheated steam in the outermost pipe melts the underground sulphur.

q: In the Frasch Process, hot air under high pressure is forced down through the innermost pipe to force the molten sulphur up the middle pipe.
e: Hot air pressure in the innermost pipe pushes the molten sulphur to the surface.

q: Sulphur obtained by the Frasch Process is 99.5% pure.
e: The textbook specifies the purity of sulphur from this process is 99.5%.

q: The oxidation number of sulphur in hydrogen sulphide ($H_2S$) is -2.
e: Table 6.3 lists the oxidation number of sulphur in $H_2S$ as -2.

q: The oxidation number of sulphur in sulphur dioxide ($SO_2$) is +6.
e: The oxidation number of sulphur in sulphur dioxide ($SO_2$) is +4.

q: The oxidation number of sulphur in sulphur trioxide ($SO_3$) is +6.
e: Table 6.3 lists the oxidation number of sulphur in $SO_3$ as +6.

q: Sulphur has two important oxides: sulphur dioxide ($SO_2$) and sulphur trioxide ($SO_3$).
e: These are the two important oxides of sulphur discussed.

q: In the laboratory, sulphur dioxide can be prepared by the reaction of sodium sulphite with dilute sulphuric acid.
e: This is one of the laboratory preparation methods for sulphur dioxide.

q: Sulphur dioxide gas is collected by the upward displacement of air.
e: Table 6.4 states sulphur dioxide is collected by upward displacement of air.

q: Sulphur dioxide is a colourless gas with a pungent odour and is very soluble in water.
e: These are the physical properties of sulphur dioxide listed in the textbook.

q: Sulphur dioxide combines with oxygen in the presence of a catalyst such as platinum or vanadium(V) oxide at 450-500°C to form sulphur trioxide.
e: This is the addition reaction of sulphur dioxide to form sulphur trioxide.

q: Sulphur dioxide directly combines with chlorine in the presence of sunlight to form sulphuryl chloride.
e: The textbook states this reaction produces sulphuryl chloride.

q: Sulphur dioxide reacts with basic oxides to form sulphates.
e: Sulphur dioxide reacts with basic oxides to form sulphites, not sulphates.

q: Sulphur dioxide reduces halogens to hydrogen halides.
e: This demonstrates the reducing property of sulphur dioxide.

q: Sulphur dioxide reduces violet coloured acidified potassium permanganate solution to a colourless solution.
e: This is a standard test showing the reducing property of sulphur dioxide.

q: Sulphur dioxide reduces orange coloured acidified potassium dichromate solution to a green solution.
e: This is another standard test showing the reducing property of sulphur dioxide.

q: The bleaching action of sulphur dioxide is due to the oxidising property of nascent hydrogen produced when it reacts with water.
e: The bleaching action of sulphur dioxide is due to the reducing property of nascent hydrogen.

q: Sulphur dioxide can oxidise magnesium and carbon monoxide.
e: The textbook lists magnesium and carbon monoxide as substances oxidised by sulphur dioxide.

q: Sulphur dioxide is used in the food industries as a food preservative and bleaching agent.
e: These are the stated uses of sulphur dioxide in the food industry.

q: In the laboratory, hydrogen sulphide gas is prepared by the action of non-oxidising acids on metal sulphides.
e: This is the standard laboratory preparation method for hydrogen sulphide.

q: Hydrogen sulphide gas is collected by the upward displacement of air because it is heavier than air.
e: The textbook states it is heavier than air and collected this way.

q: When a piece of paper soaked with lead(II) nitrate is placed near the mouth of a gas jar full of hydrogen sulphide, the paper turns black.
e: This is the test to confirm the gas jar is full of hydrogen sulphide.

q: Hydrogen sulphide is a colourless gas with a rotten egg smell and is very poisonous.
e: These are the physical properties of hydrogen sulphide.

q: In a limited supply of oxygen, hydrogen sulphide burns to produce water and sulphur dioxide.
e: In a limited supply of oxygen, hydrogen sulphide burns to produce water and sulphur.

q: In an excess of oxygen, hydrogen sulphide burns to produce water and sulphur dioxide.
e: Excess oxygen leads to the complete combustion of hydrogen sulphide to sulphur dioxide.

q: Hydrogen sulphide reacts with all metals in the reactivity series except gold and platinum.
e: Gold and platinum are the only metals in the reactivity series that do not react with hydrogen sulphide.

q: Hydrogen sulphide reduces halogens to hydrogen halides and sulphur.
e: This demonstrates the reducing property of hydrogen sulphide.

q: Hydrogen sulphide reduces acidified potassium permanganate solution to a colourless solution.
e: Hydrogen sulphide acts as a reducing agent in this reaction.

q: Hydrogen sulphide reduces acidified potassium dichromate solution to a green solution.
e: Hydrogen sulphide reduces the orange dichromate to green chromium(III) sulphate.

q: Sulphuric acid is manufactured by the Contact Process.
e: The Contact Process is the industrial method for manufacturing sulphuric acid.

q: In the Contact Process, the gas mixture of $SO_2$ and excess air is passed into a wash tower to remove impurities which might poison the catalyst.
e: Removing impurities like arsenious oxide prevents catalyst poisoning.

q: In the Contact Process, the dried sulphur dioxide and excess air are passed over a platinum or vanadium(V) oxide catalyst at 450-500°C to produce sulphur trioxide.
e: These are the exact conditions for the catalytic oxidation step.

q: Sulphur trioxide is easily dissolved in water to produce sulphuric acid directly.
e: Sulphur trioxide is dissolved in concentrated sulphuric acid to form oleum, which is then diluted with water.

q: Oleum is then diluted with water to produce sulphuric acid of any desired concentration.
e: This is the final step in the Contact Process.

q: Sulphuric acid is a colourless, oily, and heavy liquid with a density of 1.84 g/mL.
e: These are the physical properties of sulphuric acid.

q: Dilute sulphuric acid reacts with iron and metals above iron in the reactivity series, producing sulphates and hydrogen.
e: This describes the reaction of dilute sulphuric acid with reactive metals.

q: Concentrated sulphuric acid is a very powerful dehydrating agent.
e: The textbook explicitly states concentrated sulphuric acid is a powerful dehydrating agent.

q: When concentrated sulphuric acid is added to blue copper(II) sulphate pentahydrate, it becomes white anhydrous copper(II) sulphate.
e: This demonstrates the dehydrating property of concentrated sulphuric acid.

q: Sugar, starch, and other carbohydrates are dehydrated by concentrated sulphuric acid, forming carbon as the final product.
e: The dehydration of carbohydrates by concentrated sulphuric acid leaves black carbon.

q: Hot concentrated sulphuric acid oxidises metals and non-metals.
e: This describes the oxidising property of hot concentrated sulphuric acid.

q: Copper reacts with concentrated sulphuric acid to produce sulphur dioxide gas, copper(II) sulphate, and water.
e: This is the specific reaction of copper with concentrated sulphuric acid.

q: Carbon is oxidised to carbon monoxide when it reacts with hot concentrated sulphuric acid.
e: Carbon is oxidised to carbon dioxide when it reacts with hot concentrated sulphuric acid.

q: The major use of sulphuric acid is in the production of fertilisers, such as superphosphate and ammonium sulphate.
e: Fertiliser production is the major use of sulphuric acid.

q: Dilute sulphuric acid is used in lead-storage batteries.
e: The textbook states dilute sulphuric acid is used in lead-storage batteries.

q: Nitrogen is used in food packaging to keep food fresh, for example, in crisp packets.
e: This is listed under Chemistry in Society.

q: Aircrafts and car tyres are filled with nitrogen because of its reactive property.
e: Aircrafts and car tyres are filled with nitrogen because of its inert property.

q: Mineral sulphur is widely used in vulcanisation, a chemical process for converting natural rubber into more durable materials.
e: Vulcanisation with sulphur makes natural rubber more durable.

q: Sulphuric acid is used in petroleum refining to wash impurities out of gasoline and other refinery products.
e: This is a stated industrial use of sulphuric acid.

q: Sulphuric acid is used in processing metals, e.g., in pickling (cleaning) iron and steel before plating them with tin or zinc.
e: Pickling iron and steel is a stated use of sulphuric acid.

q: Nitrogen is present to the extent of about 21 percentage by volume of the air.
e: Nitrogen is present to the extent of about 78 percentage by volume of the air.

q: Nitrogen gas is relatively active and supports combustion.
e: Nitrogen gas is very unreactive and does not support combustion.

q: Sulphur is a yellow, strong smelling solid element.
e: This matches the description of sulphur in the textbook exercises.

q: Hydrogen sulphide turns blue litmus slightly red.
e: Hydrogen sulphide is slightly acidic, turning blue litmus slightly red.
